core_principles: Using an unstable load, such as a water-filled tube (slosh tube), is an effective method to create muscle instability and train for stability.
Performing a bicep curl with an unstable water-inertia implement increases instability in the paraspinal and deltoid muscles for both men and women.
Men experience greater overall instability in the biceps compared to women when using an unstable water-filled implement.
Women exhibit significantly higher muscle activation (%MVC) in the biceps and paraspinal muscles during unstable bicep curls compared to men.
specific_findings: Significant instability was seen in the paraspinal muscles for both genders at the 50% (CV= 26.5 ± 14.5) and 100% (CV= 27.1 ± 9.9) condition compared to stable (CV= 15.0 ± 9.1).
Across all subjects the deltoid showed greatest instability at the 100% open setting (CV= 38.5 ± 23.2) compared to stable (CV= 21.0 ± 7.5).
For the bicep, men showed greater overall instability (CV= 30.9 ± 17.0) compared to women (CV= 22.9 ± 8.4).

Percent MVC activated was significantly greater for women for the bicep (50% open = 97.7 ± 57.6, 100% open = 88.1 ± 55.6, stable = 87.0 ± 50.1) compared to men (50% open = 39.5 ± 17.0, 100% open = 38.3 ± 18.3, stable = 31.8 ± 11.1).

Percent MVC activated was significantly greater for women for the paraspinal muscles (50% open = 36.7 ± 22.3, 100% open = 47.5 ± 29.0, stable = 38.6 ± 23.9) compared to men (50% open = 15.1 ± 10.0, 100% open = 16.2 ± 8.8, stable = 14.3 ± 9.6).

The leg extension study utilized 8 men (age= 19.9± 1.6y, ht=178.8 ± 8.9cm, mass= 103.3 ± 48.5kg, Leg Ext 1RM= 136.5 ± 15.9kg) and 8 women (age= 20.1 ± 1.1y, ht=164.9 ± 9.8cm, mass= 62.9 ± 12.2kg, Leg Ext 1RM= 91.5 ± 15.5kg) performing trials with an 11.4 kg tube partially filled with water.
